title: Markov Chains: Modeling Customer Journeys
subtitle: Every customer is somewhere in a journey — browsing, buying, lapsing, returning. Tonight we model those journeys as Markov chains, compute lifetime value and churn, and see how the same math built Google. Plus: MIDTERM CASE DUE — team briefings tonight.

objectives.title: Model systems with states and transition matrices
objectives.description: Represent a customer base — or any evolving system — as a set of states with transition probabilities, and use matrix multiplication to project where the population will be in one month, six months, or the long run.

objectives.title: Compute steady states and long-run behavior
objectives.description: Find the equilibrium distribution a Markov chain settles into, and understand why that single vector answers questions like 'what fraction of our customers will be active a year from now?'

objectives.title: Quantify customer lifetime value and churn
objectives.description: Turn retention and churn probabilities into dollars: compute expected customer lifetime value with absorbing states, and see why a 5-point retention improvement can be worth more than a 20-point acquisition boost.

objectives.title: Apply Markov attribution to marketing spend
objectives.description: Use the removal-effect method to credit conversions across touchpoints — the Markov-chain answer to 'did the Instagram ad or the email actually close the sale?' — and understand PageRank as the same math at web scale.

agenda.title: The $200 Billion Question: Where Do Customers Go?
agenda.description: Netflix loses a subscriber. Was it forever, or a pause? Spotify sees a free user go quiet. Starbucks watches a gold-tier member drop to two visits a month. Every subscription and loyalty business lives or dies on transitions between customer states — and tonight's math prices those transitions.
bulletPoints: Opening story: why streaming services obsess over 'resurrection rates' as much as churn — lapsed customers who return cost a fraction of new acquisitions
The Markov property: the future depends only on the current state — a bold, useful simplification
States for a business: Active, At-Risk, Lapsed, Churned — how analysts actually define them from behavioral data
Tonight's arc: transition matrices → steady state → CLV → attribution → your midterm briefings

agenda.title: Transition Matrices & Steady State
agenda.description: The mechanics, live in numpy. A transition matrix P holds one row per state; multiplying a population vector by P advances the world one time step. Do it enough times and the system forgets where it started — that's the steady state.
bulletPoints: Building P: rows sum to 1, entries estimated from historical cohort data (e.g., 70% of Active customers stay Active next month)
Projection: the population after k months is x₀Pᵏ — three lines of numpy
Steady state as the eigenvector of P for eigenvalue 1 — and the power-iteration shortcut
Absorbing states: 'Churned' as a one-way door, and why absorbing chains unlock lifetime-value math

agenda.title: CLV, Attribution & the PageRank Connection
agenda.description: Three killer applications in fifteen minutes. Customer lifetime value from expected time before absorption. Marketing attribution via the removal effect — delete a channel from the journey chain and measure how many conversions vanish. And the biggest Markov chain ever built: Google's PageRank, which models a random web surfer and ranks pages by steady-state visit probability.
bulletPoints: CLV = margin per period × expected periods spent in paying states before churning
Removal effect: if deleting 'paid search' from the journey chain drops conversion probability 35%, paid search earns 35% of the credit — far fairer than last-click attribution
PageRank: a $2 trillion company founded on the steady state of a Markov chain over the web graph
Limits of the Markov property: seasonality, memory, and when you need richer models

activities.title: From Transition Matrix to Customer Lifetime Value
activities.description: Build a complete customer-journey model for a $15/month subscription business: encode the transition matrix, project the customer base, find the steady state, and convert churn math into a defensible CLV number a CFO would accept.

steps.title: Encode the journey
steps.description: Create a 4×4 numpy transition matrix over Active, At-Risk, Lapsed, and Churned (absorbing). Verify every row sums to 1 — the most common Markov bug in the wild.

steps.title: Project the cohort
steps.description: Start 10,000 customers in Active and multiply by P twelve times. How many are still active after a year? After three?

steps.title: Find the steady state
steps.description: Run power iteration until the distribution stops changing. With an absorbing Churned state, where does everyone end up eventually — and what does the transient behavior tell you instead?

steps.title: Compute CLV
steps.description: Extract the transient submatrix Q, compute the fundamental matrix N = (I − Q)⁻¹, and multiply expected months in revenue-generating states by monthly margin. Then improve Active retention by 5 points and re-run — how much is that worth per customer?

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np

states = ["Active", "At-Risk", "Lapsed", "Churned"]
P = np.array([
    [0.80, 0.15, 0.03, 0.02],   # Active
    [0.30, 0.40, 0.20, 0.10],   # At-Risk
    [0.10, 0.10, 0.50, 0.30],   # Lapsed
    [0.00, 0.00, 0.00, 1.00],   # Churned (absorbing)
])

# Project 10,000 new customers 12 months forward
x = np.array([10_000.0, 0, 0, 0])
for _ in range(12):
    x = x @ P
print(dict(zip(states, x.round())))

# CLV via the fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1
Q = P[:3, :3]                         # transient states only
N = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(3) - Q)      # expected months in each state
margin = np.array([15.0, 15.0, 0.0])  # $/month by state (Lapsed pays $0)
clv = N @ margin
print(f"CLV of a new Active customer: ${clv[0]:,.2f}")

activities.discussionNote: Your model says a new customer is worth a specific dollar amount — so what's the maximum you'd pay to acquire one? Now compare two interventions costing $2 per customer per month: one lifts Active retention from 0.80 to 0.85, the other lifts At-Risk recovery from 0.30 to 0.40. Re-run the numbers. Which wins, and would your marketing team have guessed right?

takeaways.text: A transition matrix is a complete model of system dynamics in one object: multiply to project the future, find the eigenvector to see the long run, invert (I − Q) to price the journey. Customer bases, web surfers, and machine states all obey the same algebra.

Absorbing-chain math turns retention rates into dollars: customer lifetime value is expected time in paying states times margin — which is why small retention gains routinely beat big acquisition pushes.

Removal-effect attribution and PageRank are the same idea at different scales: measure a node's importance by what breaks when you take it out of the chain. Google turned that eigenvector into the modern web.
